content:
Touma noticed the man’s hand before he noticed the boy.

The headache was already blooming.

That was the first warning.

The old transit station’s lights were too sharp. Everything seemed to have extra edges, and the vending machine’s hum was too loud.

The second warning followed: a man in a gray coat was steering a boy toward a service gate. One hand was closed around the boy’s wrist. The other stayed inside his coat.

Touma started moving.

The boy was a small-built teenager with a school bag hanging from one shoulder. The man moved with the dull confidence of someone carrying out a procedure. Around them, strangers checked departure times, watched their feet, and found reasons to look elsewhere.

The boy wasn’t struggling. His face held a blank terror, beyond pleading, as though he no longer expected anyone to understand what was happening.

Touma understood enough.

Trouble outside your head could be outrun. Trouble inside your skull came with you. He was used to trouble, and tired of it.

It was not gallantry. It was recognition.

Six steps brought him close enough.

“Hey.”

The man glanced at him without stopping.

And Touma caught the thought.

*Keep moving. Keep the kid quiet. Finish the handoff.*

It had the hard, narrow shape of an instruction. Touma touched it—not with his hands, but with something that felt like setting a paperknife to the edge of a thought.

Then he unthought it.

For an instant, the pain was a pin driven through the inside of the world.

The man’s hand opened.

The boy stumbled backward, clutching at his school bag. The man lurched as though his body had a private appointment with gravity and had only just remembered it. His other hand came out of his coat to catch the gate.

For half a second, that was enough.

The boy was free. The handoff had stopped. Touma let himself breathe.

Then the second half arrived.

His memory hiccupped.

The boy looked up at him, and Touma felt something slip. There had been familiarity in that face. He was certain of it, though he could no longer find what had made it familiar.

He searched for it and found nothing.

The boy was still standing in front of him. The school bag was still hanging from his shoulder. Nothing visible had changed.

That was the clean, quiet cruelty of it.

Touma was looking at a stranger.
